profiles.meeting_scenario: An invited planning meeting for a review article on evolutionary deep learning, where a senior faculty member and a postdoctoral researcher are organizing how to cover three promised axes: optimization/taxonomy, critical methodological analysis, and future challenges. The immediate context is that the target journal editor has asked for a detailed outline and provisional section ownership within two weeks. The agenda is to decide how to assemble the literature corpus, what the taxonomy deliverable should look like, how to handle the paper's two 'case studies,' and who will prepare which materials by next Friday. The expected outcome is an agreed plan for literature collection, section assignments, and a short-term timeline that both believe is aligned enough to start working immediately.

members.name: Dr. Elena Ruiz
members.expertise: Evolutionary computation, neural architecture search, scholarly synthesis papers
members.background: Elena leads a small ML lab, has published several survey and position papers, and was invited by the journal because of her prior work on metaheuristics for deep learning.
members.private_state: She wants a strong invited review submitted quickly, prefers a tightly scoped narrative synthesis over a labor-intensive systematic review, and hopes to delegate most evidence gathering while she focuses on framing and final writing.
hidden_assumptions: In a review paper, 'case studies' are illustrative syntheses of published application areas rather than new experiments or reproductions.
The natural scope of 'evolutionary deep learning' excludes papers where evolution mainly tunes preprocessing or feature selection around a fixed deep model.
A 'first draft' of a section means a workable outline with key citations, section headings, and rough tables that she can later rewrite.
For an invited critical review, starting from major prior surveys and then snowballing citations is the normal way to screen the literature; a formal database protocol is unnecessary.

members.name: Dr. Samir Patel
members.expertise: Reproducibility, empirical benchmarking, literature review workflows in machine learning
members.background: Samir recently finished a PhD on reproducible evaluation of optimization methods in deep learning and has experience building evidence matrices and running compact replication studies.
members.private_state: He wants the review to be methodologically defensible and visibly substantial enough to support his first-author contribution, and he worries that a loose synthesis will be criticized as selective.
hidden_assumptions: When a review promises 'case studies,' readers expect at least small in-house reruns or standardized re-analyses, not only narrative examples from prior papers.
If a deep model is the predictive core, papers where evolution optimizes surrounding pipeline components still belong inside the review's main corpus.
A 'first draft' should be coherent prose and populated tables that are ready to circulate to coauthors with minimal rewriting.
Proper literature screening means explicit query strings across databases, deduplication, and logging inclusion/exclusion decisions before citation snowballing.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the two case studies
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the paper will include 'two case studies.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means two illustrative mini-sections synthesizing representative published work in selected application areas, with no new experiments.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means two compact reproduction-style analyses where he reruns representative evolutionary deep learning methods under a shared setup.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In review writing, 'case study' is routinely used for both narrative exemplars and empirical demonstrations, so the phrase sounds fully settled even though the workload and output are very different.

misalignment_points.topic: Boundary of the core literature corpus
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss assembling the 'core corpus' of evolutionary deep learning papers.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the core corpus includes papers where evolutionary methods directly optimize deep architectures, hyperparameters, or network parameters.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the core corpus also includes hybrid pipelines where evolution selects features, preprocessing steps, or data augmentation settings around a deep learner.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both descriptions sound like obvious instances of the same field, and because neither person is proposing a specific controversial paper in the meeting, the scope boundary never gets forced into the open.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of the first draft due next Friday
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the 'taxonomy draft' or 'first draft' will be ready by next Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this means a structured outline with category labels, representative citations, and rough figure/table placeholders sufficient for planning the full manuscript.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this means a polished subsection in prose with populated tables and coded papers, suitable to circulate to coauthors.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Academic teams often use 'draft' loosely, and because both versions plausibly satisfy a near-term milestone, the apparent agreement survives without anyone asking what level of completeness is expected.

misalignment_points.topic: How the literature screening will be done
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that Samir will 'screen the literature' and build the spreadsheet.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes he will begin from existing surveys, add newer papers through backward/forward citation chasing, and track only included studies in a lightweight evidence sheet.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes he will run explicit searches in Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore, deduplicate results, and keep a traceable evidence matrix including exclusions and reason codes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both procedures are common and professional, and 'screen the literature' is a familiar umbrella phrase that hides substantial variation in effort, timing, and documentation detail.

turns.inner_thought: I need this invited piece to move fast and look authoritative. The editor wants a detailed outline soon, so today's meeting has to lock enough structure that I can frame the narrative and leave the heavier evidence gathering to Samir. The three axes are straightforward: taxonomy of evolutionary deep learning, a critical read on methodological habits, and future challenges. If he can pull together the literature and a workable taxonomy outline quickly, I can do the positioning and final prose.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Samir. Since this is an invited review, I'd like us to leave today with a firm plan around the three main axes we promised: the optimization and taxonomy piece, the critical methodological analysis, and the future challenges section. We also need a clean timeline so I can send the editor a detailed outline and provisional ownership within the next two weeks.

turns.inner_thought: Good, this can be substantial if we structure it properly. I want this to be defensible and not just another selective narrative. The backbone should be a well-defined core corpus, then coding for the taxonomy, then two case studies that make the review concrete and show some hands-on comparative analysis. If we do that well, the paper will look rigorous and my contribution will be visible.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I think the cleanest breakdown is to first assemble the core corpus of evolutionary deep learning papers, then code those papers against the taxonomy, and in parallel prepare the two case studies so the review feels grounded rather than purely abstract.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly. Fastest route is to start from the big surveys and position papers I already know, then extend from there through citation chaining. No need to bog this down with a full systematic protocol. Also, the core corpus should stay focused on work where evolution actually shapes the deep model itself, not every surrounding pipeline tweak. If we keep scope disciplined, we can write quickly and still sound comprehensive.
turns.utterance: Agreed. For speed, I'd start the core corpus from the major review papers and established surveys, then extend it with recent forward and backward snowballing. That should give us enough coverage quickly without overcomplicating the setup.

turns.inner_thought: Fine by me as a starting point, but I still need to screen broadly and document the process properly before deciding what stays in the core corpus. I want searches across the major databases, deduplication, and a traceable spreadsheet so if anyone asks how we got the set, we have an answer. Better to cast a wide net first, especially because I consider hybrid optimization around deep models part of the space too.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can take that on. I'll screen the literature broadly first and keep everything organized in the spreadsheet, then we can narrow the core corpus once the landscape is visible.

turns.inner_thought: I should pin him to a near-term deliverable. For next Friday, I really just need a usable taxonomy scaffold: category labels, representative citations, maybe a rough table layout. It doesn't need polished prose yet; I can rewrite that later. If he overdoes it, fine, but I need something lightweight enough to actually arrive on time.
turns.utterance: Great. Then let's make the taxonomy draft the first hard milestone. By next Friday, what I need is the category structure, representative citations under each bucket, and at least a sketch of the summary table so we can build the full outline around it.

turns.inner_thought: Next Friday is tight, but doable if I move fast. A draft should mean something coherent enough to circulate, not just headings. If I code the papers consistently, I can turn that into prose and a populated table the coauthors can actually react to. I just need enough breadth in the corpus to avoid making the taxonomy look arbitrary.
turns.utterance: That works. By next Friday I should be able to send a clean taxonomy draft, assuming I can get the papers coded consistently enough for the table to be shareable.

turns.inner_thought: Now the case studies. For this review, those should simply be two focused illustrative syntheses that show how the taxonomy and critique play out in recognizable subareas. CIFAR-10 architecture search is obvious, and medical imaging hyperparameter optimization gives a different flavor. Both are easy to motivate from published work without adding experimental burden.
turns.utterance: On the two case studies, I think we can make those very effective if one centers on CIFAR-10 architecture search and the other on medical imaging hyperparameter optimization. Together they should illustrate the lessons of the review quite well.

turns.inner_thought: Those are good choices because they're feasible for compact reruns and have recognizable benchmarks. If I set up a small common evaluation template, the two case studies can show method behavior in a standardized way and make the paper much stronger. This is exactly the sort of visible substance I want tied to my first-author role.
turns.utterance: Yes, those case studies are workable. I'll start thinking about them with a common comparison template in mind so they align well with the rest of the paper.

turns.inner_thought: I should make sure he doesn't turn this into a months-long systematic review. The methodological analysis should be sharp and critical, but based on patterns in the literature rather than an elaborate protocol. I want recurring flaws, common reporting weaknesses, and recommendations for the field—enough to sound substantive without slowing submission.
turns.utterance: For the methodological analysis, I'd like us to surface the recurring weaknesses and practical recommendations clearly, but without letting the project balloon into a full systematic-review exercise. The paper should stay critical and readable.

turns.inner_thought: I hear that as: keep the paper readable, but still make the underlying review process traceable. That's fine. I'll maintain explicit search records, exclusions, and coding notes in an evidence matrix so the critique doesn't look impressionistic. If reviewers push on defensibility, we'll be covered.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I'll document the search strings, exclusions, and coding notes in the evidence matrix as I screen the literature and build the spreadsheet, so the methodological analysis is easy to trace back when we write it up.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. Once his Friday draft arrives, I can turn it into the manuscript spine. I'll draft the introduction and future challenges myself and use his materials to update the editor. As long as I have a structured taxonomy draft and enough evidence to point to, we're on track.
turns.utterance: Excellent. Then once your first draft lands Friday, I'll take that and start shaping the introduction and the challenges section. We can also use that material as the basis for the editor update on scope and section ownership.

turns.inner_thought: Good. By end of week I should have an initial screening pass, a documented spreadsheet, a solid taxonomy section draft, and at least momentum on the case studies. That should demonstrate rigor and give us something concrete to circulate. I assume Elena will appreciate getting a near-finished section rather than just a skeleton.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll send the draft, the spreadsheet, and a brief case-study progress update at the end of the week, after the initial screening pass. That should give us a solid base for the next step.
